body: More than three decades ago, Hidden Valley Corporation bought two neighboring properties in Miami. It leased one to BellSouth Mobility and later gave BellSouth and its successors an easement to use part of the other for telecommunications. The easement agreement's "Remedies for Breach" section entitles the prevailing party in a suit to enforce it to reasonable attorney's fees and costs. Both properties later changed hands; when this dispute arose, RJ's International Trading, LLC (RJI) owned the burdened parcel, and Crown Castle South, LLC subleased the neighboring property from BellSouth and held the easement rights.

In 2020, Crown Castle excavated parts of RJI's land beyond the easement and installed underground fiber-optic cable. RJI sued in federal court. The district court granted RJI partial summary judgment on trespass and breach of the easement, and after a six-day trial a jury awarded $1 for the breach and $40,000 for trespass; Crown Castle did not appeal. The district court then denied RJI's motion for attorney's fees under the easement, agreeing with Crown Castle that the provision did not touch and concern the land. On RJI's appeal, the Eleventh Circuit rejected RJI's argument that it was a party to the agreement and certified the covenant question to the Florida Supreme Court.

Justice Jamie Grosshans wrote for the court. A covenant runs with the land only if the original parties intended to bind successors, successors had notice, and the covenant touches and concerns the land; the court decided the case on the third element. Tracing the doctrine from Spencer's Case (1583) through Florida decisions, it held that courts should ask whether the obligation is sufficiently connected to how the land is used, occupied or enjoyed. The fee provision does not restrict how RJI's land can be used or who can use it, and it applies only after a dispute is resolved, serving "solely to allocate litigation costs between the parties," the court wrote. It distinguished Hayslip v. U.S. Home Corp., which held that a deed's arbitration clause ran with the land, and noted that most courts outside Florida to address fee provisions agree.

Chief Justice Couriel and Justices Labarga, Muñiz and Francis concurred. Justices Barrios and Tanenbaum concurred in result only: Justice Barrios would require a direct effect on the physical use of the property and called Hayslip an outlier, and Justice Tanenbaum wrote that a prevailing-party fee provision can never be a real covenant.

timeline.label: Crown Castle excavates beyond the easement's boundaries and installs fiber-optic cable on RJI's land
Eleventh Circuit certifies the fee-provision question to the Florida Supreme Court
Florida Supreme Court answers that the easement's attorney's-fee clause does not run with the land
